text: To reproduce a teardown/recreate race, force the activity to be destroyed rather than relying on timing. First check the activity's configChanges in the manifest. If it declares none, rotating to landscape or turning on dark mode destroys and recreates the activity, the preview surface and the native engine. This is faster and more reliable than trying to time backgrounding against async work.

Retry a failing automation step, recipe or diagnosis unchanged at most once. If it fails the same way twice, change the approach or the setup. If two or three UI recipes in a row fail to reach the trigger, switch to a recipe that calls the engine directly, or one that uses a repro hook, to create the suspected state. These recipes are only for finding the trigger. Verify still needs real taps (see

Try the shortest user sequence that reaches the faulty call first, for example opening the project and doing the single action. In one case the lab showed that the earlier edits, drags and scrubs in the field log were not needed. Every extra step in a long sequence is another place where the automation can break.

Fire triggers and judge checkpoints from engine log lines (Msg... lines), not from fixed delays, UI timing, or analytics/UI event names. Arm the replay on a when_log engine line, for example a converted clip reaching the engine or the engine destructor message. Then fire the lifecycle action (home, rotate) right away, or tap the next screen that still calls the engine.

Design checkpoints and the fix so that a fixed run can still prove it reached the crash moment. Checkpoints must prove the setup, not the fault, and must come before the fix's change (the user gesture, or the engine message being sent). Do not require the faulty call itself, such as the call that sends the bad value. If an app-side fix stops sending it, the run is counted as 'trigger not reached'.

Do not guess which UI action sends an engine message. Grep the current build to find which confirmed UI action actually sends the expected engine message, and script exactly that action. Opening and leaving a tool is often not enough, because the app may send the message only after an edit is confirmed.

Check the harness API before you write a recipe module, and never guess selectors, control positions or helper signatures. The module must define every lane function the harness asks for (<name>_a(ed, r) and <name>_b(ed, r)). Selectors must use the harness syntax, for example 'id:...'. Bare names like 'mediaList' are rejected before anything runs. Check the zesty.py helper signatures before passin

To make a heavy-edit ANR, an engine-thread race or a lock-contention ANR fire, try undo/redo early. Tapping the edit's apply button three times gave no main-thread ANR. Undo/redo of the same edit gave one on the first try, because it replays the full engine reload back to back while the UI posts a blocking query. The undo control (ve_btn_undo) once failed with 'not found', so confirm its selector

Control the project/draft state and the test content, and write every recipe for the draft it will actually start from. First check that the draft meets the field crash's preconditions, such as the number of clips on the target layer and special items like freezes. The default lab-phone draft has a single long clip, so split and trim checkpoints can never fire from it. Build fixture projects that

Set up the file state before the recipe runs. Check that every host-side asset exists, or generate it at the start of the recipe. A missing repro_assets file once crashed the script with FileNotFoundError on both lanes before the trigger. Plant files into the app cache in two steps: make the asset on the host, then plant it. Wipe the app's cache dir first (clear_app_files('cache') or run-as rm).

On draft open, the app re-adds saved overlays by itself about 1 s after the draft media finishes applying, using the saved path exactly as stored. Overlays added in the editor are saved as the app's own cached transcode file, which stays on disk. To reproduce a missing or broken overlay file, edit the draft so the overlay points to a separate external file, delete that file, and reopen the draft.

Overlay tool navigation in PlayerActivity: the Overlay tab (ve_tab_overlay) is about the 10th item in the horizontal bottom bar and is off-screen on the phone, so scroll the bar before looking it up. In a draft that already has overlays, the tool does not open the gallery picker. Do not wait for gallery-only ids like deselect_button; select an existing overlay instead.

Make one attempt per app process, and make sure the old process is really gone. Start every repro cycle from a fresh process with exactly the activity stack you intend. Do not call open_draft or the open-editor/slideshow step on top of a live child screen, and do not call it again inside a recipe, because the stack it leaves will not reach the teardown checkpoint. Each reopen also kills the app.

For crashes caused by a missing Intent extra, the lab door can launch the activity directly with no extras ('launch <Activity> extras=none'). This reproduces the crash without walking the UI to the screen.

Check the environment and the code before you write any recipe. Identify the installed APK. The launcher name tells you nothing, because the lab build (developer test menu) and the Play-installed release both launch through com.myzesty/.MainActivity. Use `dumpsys package com.myzesty` and check versionCode, plus installerPackageName=com.android.vending for a Play install.

Plan for the physical phone lane to supply the clean runs needed for repro and verify. The emulator (emulator-5554) is unreliable as infrastructure: it has failed to boot within 360 s (about 40 s when it boots at all), failed its first APK install, gone offline, and never fired real row-drag gestures. Treat those infrastructure errors as noise, not as results.

On the Android 16 lab device, opening the sticker tool right after a draft loads kills the process about 0.4 s later with am_proc_died and no Java FATAL line. Avoid that path in recipes, or the run will log a FAIL_DIED unrelated to the target crash.

Judge repro and verify runs strictly and read each outcome fully. Count a lab hit as a repro, or a crash on the fixed build as a regression, only if it is the target field crash. An ANR counts only if its main-thread frames match the field. Other routes, such as draft open or back from a tool screen, can reach the same function and give a KeyEvent ANR with a different stack.

The root-cause self-check rejects claims that hold for only one event: timings, error order, or errors missing from other events. Each rejection costs a redo round of about 2 minutes, and such claims have already cost two rounds. Before submitting, check that every timing, error and step in the trigger appears in every event, and keep single-event claims out of the main story.

A verify recipe must replay exactly the path that crashed, with real taps, and you must prove it reliable before the propose step. Hook or direct-engine recipes are for finding the trigger, not for verify. When an earlier recipe already hit the crash in the lab, copy its setup steps exactly instead of writing new ones. Watch for recipes that randomize per seed, for example leaving by back key or t

Patches (fixes and repro hooks) must apply to and compile against the tree the lab actually builds, not the main checkout or current branch. A candidate whose patch fails to apply is thrown out of the tournament before anyone judges it. Lab builds swap in the field-commit (shipped release) versions of the files on the crash stack, and fix rounds build on the fallback lab tree. Write every diff wit

Remove trailing commas and other punctuation from any path or id taken from a log line or checkpoint regex before using it in a shell command. A trailing ',' once made every stat fail and wasted a whole build-and-run cycle.

Budget lab time realistically. An engine verify round takes about 40-45 minutes: about 1.5 minutes for the incremental arm64 build, then 2 + 6 scenario runs that each stop at about 300 s (4-5 minutes per run). A real-tap verify run takes about 3 minutes. A natural focus run with a long clip took about 225 s, so 3 repeats cost about 11 minutes. A Java/Kotlin-only fix rebuilds faster.

Choose where to put the fix by crash type. For use-after-teardown or null-object crashes, fix it once at the shared getter, or make the owner live for the whole process. This matters most when many JNI entry points reach the null owner. A guard that only makes the faulting function return a default value (0, empty, null, or a thrown exception) often just moves the crash somewhere else.

Fix both levels in the first proposal. If the engine crashed because the app sent a wrong call or stale state, such as a stale index or id from a Kotlin screen's own copy of a list, the proposal must contain the caller fix as the real fix. The engine or crash-site guard is only a second layer of hardening. Patches that only hardened the crashing engine code, constructor or decoder did not fix the

For an ANR where the main thread waits on the engine message thread, propose from the start a fix that does one of two things: move the slow decoder or render work off the message thread, or stop the main thread from waiting on it synchronously. Skipping one redundant UI call, or adding a timeout or back-off around the blocking codec call, can pass the lab and still be rejected by review.

Two harness notes are known and harmless, not failures. 'wizard Full Editor leaves an empty control area; project reopened from My Projects' appears on every run as a known workaround. 'could not leave editor cleanly: did not get back to My Projects' still lets the run pass, and the next run starts fresh. Neither needs a workaround. Passing the lab does not finish the job. In one case the patch passed the lab in all three rounds, but the independent review still found 4 to 6 blocking items each time. If the reviewer approves the design and lists blocking items, the next round should change only those items on the verified patch. Re-running a full tournament can switch to a different candidate and bring in new blocking items.

If the fix edits the same lines as the repro debug hook, the harness has to place the hook by its surrounding context. Keep the fix's edits a few lines away from the hook site, or keep the hook's context lines unchanged, so the repro hook still lands and still fires.

When an ANR is stuck inside a system call that rarely blocks, use a debug-property hook that forces the stall, together with the CPU-load boost. This makes the repro fire reliably through the real UI. It gave a 75% hit rate, so 2 runs plus 1 extra were enough for 95% confidence. Write the root cause so it says the stall was hook-induced.
